screens.title: Descriptors
screens.narratorSegment: Descriptors let an object intercept attribute access, assignment, and deletion by implementing one or more special methods. They are the mechanism beneath familiar Python features such as the property decorator, bound methods, classmethod and staticmethod. In practice, a descriptor is an object that implements get, set, or delete. When Python finds such an object in a class dictionary, it calls the corresponding method instead of returning the object directly. That indirection is powerful: it lets you enforce validation, lazily compute values, or integrate attributes with external resources. A concrete example is a TypeChecked descriptor that validates types on assignment and stores values in the instance dictionary. Common mistakes include storing state on the descriptor itself, which creates shared state across instances. This lesson will walk you through the protocol, attribute lookup order, set_name behavior, data versus non-data descriptors, and practical patterns like ReadOnly and property-backed attributes. Keep an eye out for when instance is None — that signals class-level access and often returns the descriptor itself. By the end you will understand when descriptors simplify design and when they add unnecessary complexity.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Descriptors

Descriptors

Intercept attribute access to run custom logic on get, set, or delete.

In this lesson

Why descriptors exist, the protocol methods, common pitfalls, and hands-on patterns.

Why it matters

They give reusable control for validation, lazy loading, and framework integrations like ORMs.

Explore key topics
Protocol Methods
__get__, __set__, __delete__ are the interception points.
Use Cases
Validation, lazy loading, ORMs, and read-only attributes.
Property
@property is a built-in descriptor implementing get/set/deleter methods.
Concept map
Descriptor Object
Implements one or more of the special methods to manage attribute access.
Instance Storage
Values should be stored in instance.__dict__ to avoid shared state across instances.
Data vs Non-Data
Data descriptors implement __set__ and take precedence over instance attributes.
Quick example
class TypeChecked:
  def __init__(self, expected_type):
    self.expected_type = expected_type
    self._name = None

  def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
    self._name = name

  def __get__(self, instance, owner):
    if instance is None:
      return self
    return instance.__dict__.get(self._name, None)

  def __set__(self, instance, value):
    if not isinstance(value, self.expected_type):
      raise TypeError("Expected type mismatch")
    instance.__dict__[self._name] = value

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn to define and implement descriptors, and to read the attribute lookup rules that make descriptors work. First, you'll be able to define what a descriptor is and explain why implementing get, set, or delete makes an object into one. Next, you will implement custom descriptors, walking through set_name and the practical need to store per-instance values rather than on the descriptor itself. You'll also explore how the property decorator uses the descriptor protocol, giving you a familiar pattern to connect to. Finally, you'll examine when descriptors are the right tool — for validation, lazy loading, ORMs, or managed resources — and when plain attributes are simpler. Each skill combines a short definition with a small code or design example so you can see the pattern in practice. By the end you can justify using a descriptor, implement it safely, and avoid common shared-state mistakes.

screens.title: What is a descriptor?
screens.narratorSegment: A descriptor is any object that implements one or more of the protocol methods: get, set, or delete. The key claim is that placing such an object in a class definition changes how attribute access behaves: Python will call the descriptor methods instead of simply returning the stored object. This allows you to run logic at attribute access time. For example, a descriptor can validate values on assignment, lazily compute and cache a value on first access, or forward reads and writes to external resources. A common pattern is to store per-instance values in instance. dict using a key learned from set_name. When get receives instance as None, the access is occurring on the class rather than on an instance; many descriptors return themselves in that case so introspection remains possible. A typical misconception is thinking descriptors must be complicated; in many cases they are simple helper objects that centralize behavior across many attributes. Another pitfall is putting instance state on the descriptor itself, which leads to shared state across all instances. To check understanding, ask whether a function defined in a class is a descriptor — it is, because it implements get, but it is generally a non-data descriptor. The core takeaway: descriptors are a minimal protocol for controlled attribute access and they unlock patterns that plain attributes cannot express cleanly.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A descriptor implements __get__, __set__, and/or __delete__ to control attribute behavior when placed on a class.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › What is a descriptor?
Core claim

If an object stored on a class implements __get__, __set__, or __delete__, Python routes attribute access to those methods. That single rule explains how property, bound methods, and other managed attributes behave.

Example
A TypeChecked descriptor can validate types on assignment and store the value in instance.__dict__ under a name learned from __set_name__.
Common mistake
Storing values as attributes on the descriptor creates shared state across all instances. Use instance.__dict__ instead.
Key takeaway
Descriptors provide controlled, reusable attribute behavior when you need logic on access, assignment, or deletion.
Annotated view
Descriptor object
Implements the protocol methods to intercept operations.
Instance storage
values stored in instance.__dict__ keep state per-instance.
Class-level access
When instance is None in __get__, return the descriptor to support introspection.
Check your understanding
Is a plain function defined on a class a descriptor? Yes: functions implement __get__, making them non-data descriptors that produce bound methods on instance access.

screens.title: Attribute lookup order
screens.narratorSegment: Python follows a defined order when resolving attributes. First, it checks whether the attribute name in the class dictionary refers to a descriptor object. If that object implements get or set, the descriptor protocol controls access. If Python finds a data descriptor — one that implements set or delete in addition to get — it takes precedence over any entry in instance. dict. If no descriptor is found, Python looks in the instance dictionary for the attribute value. If absent there, it falls back to the class dictionary for non-descriptor objects and then to base classes. Understanding this order is crucial to avoid surprises: for example, assigning a value to instance. dict will not override a data descriptor, but it will override a non-data descriptor that only implements get. An easy way to remember is: data descriptors first, then instance dictionary, then non-data class attributes, and finally inheritance. A common misconception is assuming instance assignment always wins; it does not when a data descriptor is present. When debugging, inspect the class dictionary and check whether an attribute implements set to predict runtime behavior.

keyIdea.title: Lookup rule
keyIdea.text: Data descriptors (with __set__) win over instance values; non-data descriptors (__get__ only) can be shadowed by instance entries.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Attribute lookup order
Ordered steps
  1. Data descriptor in the class dict (implements __set__ or __delete__) — takes precedence.
  2. Instance dictionary entry, if no data descriptor blocked it.
  3. Non-data descriptor in the class dict (implements only __get__).
  4. Plain class attribute or attributes found in base classes.
Practical debugging tip
Inspect owner.__dict__ for an attribute and check whether it implements __set__. That tells you whether instance assignment will be effective.
Misconception
Instance assignment does not always override class-level behavior when a data descriptor is present. Expect interception when __set__ exists.
Visual process
Data descriptor
Always wins. Example: a TypeChecked descriptor with __set__.
Instance dict
Normal stored values which can shadow non-data descriptors.
Non-data descriptor
Methods are an example; they implement __get__ but not __set__.
Reflection question
If a descriptor blocks instance writes, how would you add a per-instance override? Consider removing the descriptor or changing it to a non-data descriptor.

screens.title: __get__ semantics
screens.narratorSegment: get is invoked when an attribute access would otherwise return the descriptor object from the class dictionary. It accepts two arguments: the instance where the access occurred and the owner class. When you access the attribute from an instance, instance is that instance and the descriptor usually returns a value drawn from instance. dict or a computed value. When you access the attribute on the class itself, instance is None. In that class-level case, many descriptors return the descriptor object itself to allow introspection or to expose descriptor methods. A concrete example: TypeChecked. get returns self when instance is None so that Person. name returns the descriptor object, but p. name returns the stored string value. Another practical use of get is to implement bound methods: functions defined on a class implement get to produce a function bound to the instance. A common misconception is that get must always read instance. dict; it can compute values or lazily initialize them. The takeaway: check instance for None to differentiate class-level versus instance-level behavior, and design get to return either the descriptor or the per-instance value depending on that context.

keyIdea.title: __get__ rule
keyIdea.text: If instance is None, treat access as class-level; often return the descriptor itself. Otherwise, return the instance-specific value or compute it.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › __get__ semantics
Behavior rules
  • __get__(self, instance, owner) is called on attribute access.
  • If instance is None, callers are using the class; often return self for introspection.
  • Otherwise, return a per-instance value, compute on demand, or create a bound object.
Example pattern
Return self when instance is None, otherwise return instance.__dict__.get(self._name, None) or compute and cache lazily.
Misconception
Do not assume __get__ always returns the descriptor. It usually returns the descriptor on class access, but on instance access it should provide usable values or bound objects.
Concrete scenario
Bound methods
Functions implement __get__ to return a function object bound to the instance, explaining why methods receive self.
Lazy compute
__get__ can compute a value on first access and store it in instance.__dict__ so subsequent reads are cheap.
Takeaway
Always check the instance argument inside __get__ to decide whether to return the descriptor or an instance value.

screens.title: Implementing __set__ safely
screens.narratorSegment: When you implement set, the most important decision is where to store the assigned value. A common but dangerous approach is to store the value on the descriptor instance itself. That makes the attribute effectively shared across all owner instances. The safer pattern is to store the value in the instance's own dictionary using a name learned from set_name. For example, a TypeChecked descriptor captures the attribute name in set_name and then uses instance. dict[self._name] = value inside set. This keeps state per-instance and ensures assignments on one object do not affect others. Also, set should perform validation or transformation before storing the value, and it may raise TypeError or ValueError to enforce invariants. When implementing set, consider thread-safety if objects are mutated concurrently and prefer explicit error messages to aid debugging. A short code walkthrough demonstrates the pattern and contrasts the wrong approach of self. value = value with the correct instance. dict assignment to make the behavior predictable and correct. Implementing __set__ safely means store assigned values in instance.__dict__ under the attribute name captured by __set_name__ to maintain per-instance state.. In practical terms, store values per-instance and avoid shared state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Store assigned values in instance.__dict__ under the attribute name captured by __set_name__ to maintain per-instance state.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Implementing __set__
Pattern

Capture the attribute name in __set_name__, validate in __set__, and store the value in instance.__dict__[self._name]. This ensures per-instance storage and predictable behavior.

class TypeChecked:
  def __init__(self, expected_type):
    self.expected_type = expected_type
    self._name = None

  def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
    self._name = name

  def __get__(self, instance, owner):
    if instance is None:
      return self
    return instance.__dict__.get(self._name, None)

  def __set__(self, instance, value):
    if not isinstance(value, self.expected_type):
      raise TypeError(f"Expected {self.expected_type.__name__}, got {type(value).__name__}")
    instance.__dict__[self._name] = value
Wrong approach
Assigning self.value = value stores state on the descriptor object itself, making the attribute shared across all owner instances.
Concrete example
Person example
Person.name = TypeChecked(str) stores each person's name in their own __dict__ key, preventing cross-instance leakage.
Key takeaway
Use instance.__dict__ to keep attributes instance-local; use descriptor attributes only for metadata like expected_type or _name.

screens.title: __delete__ and deletion rules
screens.narratorSegment: delete is called when you execute the delete operation on a descriptor-managed attribute. Implementing delete allows the descriptor to remove per-instance state, close resources, or enforce invariants when a deletion happens. For example, a TypeChecked descriptor can implement delete to remove the key from instance. dict. If deletion is not allowed for a particular attribute, delete should raise AttributeError with a clear message; this is useful for ReadOnly descriptors where deletion is explicitly forbidden. A frequent confusion arises around the semantics of deleting class-level versus instance-level attributes. Deleting a class attribute removes the descriptor from the class dictionary, while calling del on an instance attribute triggers the descriptor's delete only if the descriptor is a data descriptor present in the class. If a descriptor's delete removes the stored value from instance. dict, subsequent reads will return the descriptor default or None depending on get implementation. When designing delete, consider whether deletion must free external resources or simply clear cached data, and ensure error messages help callers understand why deletion failed. __delete__ and deletion rules means use __delete__ to remove per-instance state or to raise attributeerror when deletion should be forbidden, like in read-only patterns.. In practical terms, how deletion is routed and when to raise errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › __delete__ and deletion rules
Use and behavior

Implement __delete__ to remove the stored value from the instance or to manage cleanup of external resources. If deletion is not permitted, raise AttributeError with a meaningful message so callers understand why the operation fails.

Practical rule
If you stored the value in instance.__dict__ under the key gathered from __set_name__, __delete__ should delete that key to restore the pre-assignment state.
ReadOnly example
A ReadOnly descriptor should implement __delete__ to raise AttributeError to prevent deletion of protected attributes.
Example
TypeChecked.__delete__
del instance.attribute should remove instance.__dict__[name] or raise KeyError if absent; handle errors to give clearer messages.
Takeaway
Design deletion semantics explicitly: either remove stored state or prevent deletion with an informative error.

screens.title: __set_name__ (Python 3.6+)
screens.narratorSegment: set_name is a convenience hook introduced in Python three.6 that the interpreter calls automatically when a descriptor is assigned as a class attribute. The method signature receives the owner class and the attribute name, letting the descriptor capture the key it should use when storing per-instance values. This solves the problem of assigning a descriptor to different names in different classes or renaming attributes later. For example, TypeChecked. set_name(self, owner, name) can set self._name = name, and later get and set use that key into instance. dict. Without set_name, descriptors often require manual configuration or rely on naming conventions. set_name keeps descriptors reusable and class-agnostic. A common subtlety: set_name is only called when the descriptor is defined at class creation time, not when you later assign a descriptor to a class attribute at runtime. Use set_name for predictable per-instance keys and to avoid fragile string-based naming hacks. This small hook reduces boilerplate and improves clarity of descriptor implementations. __set_name__ (Python 3.6+) means use __set_name__ to automatically capture the attribute name so you can store values in instance.__dict__ reliably.. In practical terms, how descriptors learn the attribute name they manage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › __set_name__
Why __set_name__ exists

It is called at class creation and gives the descriptor the attribute name so that later __get__ and __set__ can store values under a consistent key in instance.__dict__. This removes fragile naming conventions and makes descriptors reusable across classes.

Behavior note
__set_name__ is not invoked when you assign a descriptor to a class attribute at runtime after class creation. Rely on it only for class-time assignments.
Concrete usage
Capture key
def __set_name__(self, owner, name): self._name = name — later use instance.__dict__[self._name]
Takeaway
Prefer __set_name__ to hard-coded keys; it makes descriptors robust when reused or subclassed.

screens.title: Data descriptors vs Non-data descriptors
screens.narratorSegment: Descriptors split into two practical categories. Data descriptors implement set or delete in addition to get, and they take precedence during attribute lookup. This means that if a data descriptor exists for an attribute name, instance assignments to that name will invoke the descriptor instead of simply replacing the instance dictionary entry. Non-data descriptors implement only get. They provide behavior on read but can be shadowed by values in the instance dictionary. A common example: methods are non-data descriptors because they implement get to produce bound methods, but ordinary assignment to the instance will replace the method name in the instance dictionary. Understanding this difference helps explain surprising behavior: if you intended instance-level overriding but your attribute is a data descriptor, the descriptor continues to intercept assignments. Use data descriptors for strong control — validation, managed writes — and non-data descriptors when you only want to control reads. A short mental rule: if you need to control assignment or deletion, implement set or delete and accept that your descriptor will win the lookup battle. Data descriptor
Implements __set__ or __delete__. It takes precedence over instance.__dict__ entries. Use when you must enforce invariants on write.

screens.title: @property as a descriptor
screens.narratorSegment: The built-in property decorator is implemented as a descriptor. When you declare a property with a getter and optional setter and deleter, Python creates an object that implements get, set and delete as appropriate. Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › @property as a descriptor
Mapping

When you declare a property with getter and setter, Python constructs an object that implements the descriptor protocol. Its __get__ calls the getter, __set__ calls the setter, and __delete__ calls the deleter if provided.

class Circle:
  def __init__(self, radius):
    self._radius = radius

  @property
  def radius(self):
    return self._radius

  @radius.setter
  def radius(self, value):
    if value < 0:
      raise ValueError('Radius cannot be negative')
    self._radius = value
Practical note
Why use property
It provides an attribute-like interface while enabling validation and computed values under the hood via the descriptor protocol.
Takeaway
Recognizing property as a descriptor helps you reuse patterns and build your own managed attributes when needed.

screens.title: When to use descriptors
screens.narratorSegment: Descriptors shine when attributes need consistent, reusable behavior across many classes or fields. Use them to enforce validation rules — for example, TypeChecked ensures that values assigned to name or age are of the expected types. They work well for lazy loading: a descriptor can compute a value on first access and cache it in instance. dict to avoid repeated expensive computations. ORMs frequently use descriptors to map Python attributes to database columns, centralizing conversion and persistence logic. Descriptors are also useful for wrapping access to external resources, where reads or writes trigger network calls or resource acquisition. However, descriptors add indirection. For simple one-off attributes, plain properties or explicit getter/setter methods may be clearer. Consider complexity and testability: if your attribute logic is large, test the descriptor separately as a reuse unit. The practical design pattern is to encapsulate behavior in a small descriptor class, keep per-instance state in instance. dict, and document the descriptor's public contract so other developers know what to expect. Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › ReadOnly descriptor
Starter code
class ReadOnly:
  def __init__(self, default_value=None):
    self._value = default_value
    self._name = None
    self._is_set = False

  def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
    self._name = name

  def __get__(self, instance, owner):
    if instance is None:
      return self
    return instance.__dict__.get(self._name, self._value)

  def __set__(self, instance, value):
    # TODO: implement one-time set logic
    pass

  def __delete__(self, instance):
    raise AttributeError(f"Cannot delete read-only attribute '{self._name}'")
Hint
Check if self._name is already in instance.__dict__ to decide whether to allow assignment.
Solution template
def __set__(self, instance, value):
  if self._name in instance.__dict__:
    raise AttributeError(f"Cannot reassign read-only attribute '{self._name}'")
  instance.__dict__[self._name] = value
Testing
Construct an owner instance, set the attribute once, then verify that reassignment and deletion raise AttributeError. Create another instance to show independent per-instance behavior.

screens.title: Pitfalls and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When adopting descriptors, watch for a few recurring pitfalls. First, avoid storing per-instance data on the descriptor object itself — this produces shared state across instances and surprises during debugging. Second, be explicit about error types: raise TypeError or ValueError on validation failures, and raise AttributeError when write or delete operations are forbidden so caller code can handle attribute semantics consistently. Third, test descriptors independently from owner classes: unit tests that exercise get, set, and delete on a mock owner confirm correctness. Fourth, document the descriptor's contract: whether it raises on reassign, whether it uses defaults, and what keys it stores in instance. dict. Fifth, prefer simple properties for single-use cases to keep code straightforward. Finally, inspect the class dictionary when behavior is unexpected: check owner. dict[name] to see whether the attribute is a descriptor and whether it implements set, which explains precedence. These practices reduce accidental shared state, make failures clearer, and keep descriptor designs maintainable. fullNarratorScript:
Descriptors let an object intercept attribute access, assignment, and deletion by implementing one or more special methods. They are the mechanism beneath familiar Python features such as the property decorator, bound methods, classmethod and staticmethod. In practice, a descriptor is an object that implements get, set, or delete. When Python finds such an object in a class dictionary, it calls the corresponding method instead of returning the object directly. That indirection is powerful: it lets you enforce validation, lazily compute values, or integrate attributes with external resources. A concrete example is a TypeChecked descriptor that validates types on assignment and stores values in the instance dictionary. Common mistakes include storing state on the descriptor itself, which creates shared state across instances. This lesson will walk you through the protocol, attribute lookup order, set_name behavior, data versus non-data descriptors, and practical patterns like ReadOnly and property-backed attributes. Keep an eye out for when instance is None — that signals class-level access and often returns the descriptor itself. By the end you will understand when descriptors simplify design and when they add unnecessary complexity.

In this chapter you will learn to define and implement descriptors, and to read the attribute lookup rules that make descriptors work. First, you'll be able to define what a descriptor is and explain why implementing get, set, or delete makes an object into one. Next, you will implement custom descriptors, walking through set_name and the practical need to store per-instance values rather than on the descriptor itself. You'll also explore how the property decorator uses the descriptor protocol, giving you a familiar pattern to connect to. Finally, you'll examine when descriptors are the right tool — for validation, lazy loading, ORMs, or managed resources — and when plain attributes are simpler. Each skill combines a short definition with a small code or design example so you can see the pattern in practice. By the end you can justify using a descriptor, implement it safely, and avoid common shared-state mistakes.

This second objectives page emphasizes practical skills you will practice. You will learn to read attribute lookup order so you can predict when a descriptor is called versus when Python reads instance data. You will practice implementing set_name so the descriptor knows which instance dictionary key to use. You will compare data and non-data descriptors and therefore understand precedence — why a data descriptor can block an instance value. Finally, you'll apply these ideas in a short coding exercise to build a ReadOnly descriptor, which is a common pattern for configuration or metadata that should not be reassigned. Each objective ties directly back to a short coding example or a debugging checklist so you can verify behavior in a REPL or small script. By the end of these hands-on milestones you will be ready to add descriptors safely to your designs and to explain their runtime effects to a teammate.

A descriptor is any object that implements one or more of the protocol methods: get, set, or delete. The key claim is that placing such an object in a class definition changes how attribute access behaves: Python will call the descriptor methods instead of simply returning the stored object. This allows you to run logic at attribute access time. For example, a descriptor can validate values on assignment, lazily compute and cache a value on first access, or forward reads and writes to external resources. A common pattern is to store per-instance values in instance. dict using a key learned from set_name. When get receives instance as None, the access is occurring on the class rather than on an instance; many descriptors return themselves in that case so introspection remains possible. A typical misconception is thinking descriptors must be complicated; in many cases they are simple helper objects that centralize behavior across many attributes. Another pitfall is putting instance state on the descriptor itself, which leads to shared state across all instances. To check understanding, ask whether a function defined in a class is a descriptor — it is, because it implements get, but it is generally a non-data descriptor. The core takeaway: descriptors are a minimal protocol for controlled attribute access and they unlock patterns that plain attributes cannot express cleanly.

Python follows a defined order when resolving attributes. First, it checks whether the attribute name in the class dictionary refers to a descriptor object. If that object implements get or set, the descriptor protocol controls access. If Python finds a data descriptor — one that implements set or delete in addition to get — it takes precedence over any entry in instance. dict. If no descriptor is found, Python looks in the instance dictionary for the attribute value. If absent there, it falls back to the class dictionary for non-descriptor objects and then to base classes. Understanding this order is crucial to avoid surprises: for example, assigning a value to instance. dict will not override a data descriptor, but it will override a non-data descriptor that only implements get. An easy way to remember is: data descriptors first, then instance dictionary, then non-data class attributes, and finally inheritance. A common misconception is assuming instance assignment always wins; it does not when a data descriptor is present. When debugging, inspect the class dictionary and check whether an attribute implements set to predict runtime behavior.

get is invoked when an attribute access would otherwise return the descriptor object from the class dictionary. It accepts two arguments: the instance where the access occurred and the owner class. When you access the attribute from an instance, instance is that instance and the descriptor usually returns a value drawn from instance. dict or a computed value. When you access the attribute on the class itself, instance is None. In that class-level case, many descriptors return the descriptor object itself to allow introspection or to expose descriptor methods. A concrete example: TypeChecked. get returns self when instance is None so that Person. name returns the descriptor object, but p. name returns the stored string value. Another practical use of get is to implement bound methods: functions defined on a class implement get to produce a function bound to the instance. A common misconception is that get must always read instance. dict; it can compute values or lazily initialize them. The takeaway: check instance for None to differentiate class-level versus instance-level behavior, and design get to return either the descriptor or the per-instance value depending on that context.

When you implement set, the most important decision is where to store the assigned value. A common but dangerous approach is to store the value on the descriptor instance itself. That makes the attribute effectively shared across all owner instances. The safer pattern is to store the value in the instance's own dictionary using a name learned from set_name. For example, a TypeChecked descriptor captures the attribute name in set_name and then uses instance. dict[self._name] = value inside set. This keeps state per-instance and ensures assignments on one object do not affect others. Also, set should perform validation or transformation before storing the value, and it may raise TypeError or ValueError to enforce invariants. When implementing set, consider thread-safety if objects are mutated concurrently and prefer explicit error messages to aid debugging. A short code walkthrough demonstrates the pattern and contrasts the wrong approach of self. value = value with the correct instance. dict assignment to make the behavior predictable and correct. Implementing __set__ safely means store assigned values in instance.__dict__ under the attribute name captured by __set_name__ to maintain per-instance state.. In practical terms, store values per-instance and avoid shared state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

delete is called when you execute the delete operation on a descriptor-managed attribute. Implementing delete allows the descriptor to remove per-instance state, close resources, or enforce invariants when a deletion happens. For example, a TypeChecked descriptor can implement delete to remove the key from instance. dict. If deletion is not allowed for a particular attribute, delete should raise AttributeError with a clear message; this is useful for ReadOnly descriptors where deletion is explicitly forbidden. A frequent confusion arises around the semantics of deleting class-level versus instance-level attributes. Deleting a class attribute removes the descriptor from the class dictionary, while calling del on an instance attribute triggers the descriptor's delete only if the descriptor is a data descriptor present in the class. If a descriptor's delete removes the stored value from instance. dict, subsequent reads will return the descriptor default or None depending on get implementation. When adopting descriptors, watch for a few recurring pitfalls. Third, test descriptors independently from owner classes: unit tests that exercise get, set, and delete on a mock owner confirm correctness.
